title: Charged particles in a magnetic field: practice
search_keywords: F = qvB, charged particle, circular path, velocity selector, mass spectrometer, Hall effect, charge to mass ratio, past papers
ican: I can show that v = E ÷ B in a velocity selector.
I can explain how a charged particle moves in a magnetic field.

cloze.title: Say it the exam way
cloze.text:
A charged particle moving at right angles to a magnetic field feels a force [[F = qvB|F = qv/B]]. The force is always at [[90°|0°]] to the velocity. So the speed [[stays the same|increases]] and the path is a [[circle|parabola]]. From qvB = mv²/r, a faster particle moves in a [[larger|smaller]] circle.

If the velocity also has a part along the field, the path is a [[helix|circle]]. In a velocity selector, the electric and magnetic forces are [[balanced|both zero]]. Only particles with v = [[E/B|B/E]] pass straight through.

paper2.alt: A mass spectrometer is an instrument that is used to investigate some properties of charged particles. Figure 14A shows the path of an ion from an ion source through a velocity selector into a deflection field. (b) The mass spectrometer is now used to investigate the paths followed by two types of hydrogen ion. Data: deuterium, mass 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; tritium, mass 5.01 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. These ions enter the deflection field with the velocity determined in (a)(ii) and follow semi-circular paths. One type of ion leaves the field at point Y and the other at point Z, a distance Δx apart, as shown in Figure 14C. The magnetic induction in the deflection field is 0.65 T. The radius of the curved path is given by r = mv ÷ qB. Determine the separation Δx of the ions when they leave the deflection field. 4 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2025 Question 14(b), 4 marks: r = mv ÷ qB; r for deuterium = 3.34 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2.13 × 10⁶ ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.65) (1); r for tritium = 5.01 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2.13 × 10⁶ ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.65) (1); Δx = 2 × (r tritium − r deuterium) (1); Δx = 0.068 m (1). Accept 0.07, 0.0684, 0.06841. Or consistent with (a)(ii).

paper2.lead: Part (a)(ii) was done in class. It gave the velocity: 2.13 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

paper2.alt: (c) Alpha particles with a specific speed are used to probe the nuclei of copper atoms in a target. A sample of Po-212 emits alpha particles with a range of speeds. A velocity selector allows only alpha particles with a specific speed to pass straight through to the target, as shown in Figure 8A. (i) The velocity selector has a uniform electric field and a uniform magnetic field, perpendicular to each other and to the initial velocity v of the alpha particles, as shown in Figure 8B: parallel plates with the magnetic field into the page between them. (A) Calculate the speed of an alpha particle with kinetic energy 8.8 MeV. 4 marks. (B) By considering the forces acting on an alpha particle in the velocity selector, show that the speed v of the particle travelling straight through is given by v = E ÷ B. 2 marks. (C) The potential difference between the parallel plates is 27 kV. The plate separation is 15 mm. Determine the magnetic induction that allows alpha particles with kinetic energy 8.8 MeV to pass straight through the velocity selector. 3 marks. (d) A second alpha particle with kinetic energy greater than 8.8 MeV enters the velocity selector. On Figure 8D, draw the path taken by this alpha particle in the velocity selector. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2021 Question 8(c)(i) and (d). (A) 4 marks: Ek = ½mv² (1); 8.8 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.5 × 6.645 × 10⁻²⁷ × v² (1, 1); v = 2.1 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (1). Independent mark for converting MeV to J. Accept 2, 2.06, 2.059. (B) 2 marks, show question: F = QE and F = qvB; QE = qvB (1, 1); v = E ÷ B. The final relationship must be shown, or 1 mark at most. (C) 3 marks: E = V ÷ d (1); v = E ÷ B; 2.1 × 10⁷ = (27 × 10³ ÷ 15 × 10⁻³) ÷ B (1); B = 8.6 × 10⁻² T (1). Accept 9, 8.57, 8.571. Or consistent with (A). (d) 1 mark: path drawn as an upward curve in the magnetic field. Ignore any path drawn to the right of the parallel plates.

paper2.lead: Part (A) was done in the Electric Fields deck. It gives the speed that (C) needs.

paper2.alt: A small, thin, rectangular metal plate is connected to a d.c. power supply, as shown in Figure 15A. Electrons move through the plate from left to right. A uniform magnetic field is now applied at right angles to the plate, as shown in Figure 15B. As the electrons enter the plate they experience a force due to the magnetic field. This causes the electrons to follow a curved path downwards and gather at the bottom of the plate. (a) Determine whether the direction of the magnetic field is into the page or out of the page. 1 mark. (b) After a short time, the bottom of the plate becomes negatively charged relative to the top, as shown in Figure 15C. This causes a uniform electric field between the top and bottom of the plate. Electrons moving at a fixed speed, called the drift velocity, now travel horizontally across the plate, as the electric and magnetic forces on them are balanced. (i) Show that the drift velocity is given by v = V ÷ Bd, where V is the potential difference between the top and bottom of the plate, B is the magnetic induction and d is the height of the plate. 3 marks. (ii) The plate has a height of 3.25 × 10⁻² m. The magnetic induction is 1.25 T. The potential difference between the top and bottom of the plate is 3.47 × 10⁻⁶ V. Calculate the drift velocity of the electrons. 2 marks. (iii) The magnetic induction is now increased. The drift velocity of the electrons remains the same. Explain why the drift velocity does not change. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2019 Question 15. (a) 1 mark: into the page. (b)(i) 3 marks, show question: F = QE and F = qvB (1); EQ = qvB (1); E = vB; V = Ed (1); v = V ÷ Bd. The final line must appear, or 2 marks at most. (ii) 2 marks: v = V ÷ Bd = 3.47 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ (1.25 × 3.25 × 10⁻²) (1); v = 8.54 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹ (1). Accept 8.5, 8.542, 8.5415. (iii) 2 marks, independent: more charges are separated across the plate, or more electrons gather on the bottom of the plate (1); the bigger magnetic force increases the electric force, potential difference or electric field strength across the plate (1).

paper2.alt: A student carries out an experiment to determine the charge to mass ratio of the electron. Figure 14A shows an electron gun, Helmholtz coils with an ammeter and supply, and the electron beam. An electron beam is produced using an electron gun connected to a 5.0 kV supply. A current I in the Helmholtz coils produces a uniform magnetic field. The path of the beam between points O and P is an arc of a circle of constant radius r, shown in Figure 14B. Measurements: electron gun supply voltage V = 5.0 kV (plus or minus 10%); current in the Helmholtz coils I = 0.22 A (plus or minus 5%); radius of curvature r = 0.28 m (plus or minus 6%). (a) The manufacturer's instruction sheet states that B = 4.20 × 10⁻³ × I. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field strength in the centre of the apparatus. 1 mark. (b) The charge to mass ratio is calculated using q ÷ m = 2V ÷ B²r². (i) Using the measurements recorded by the student, calculate the charge to mass ratio of the electron. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2018 Question 14(a) and (b)(i). (a) 1 mark: B = 4.2 × 10⁻³ × 0.22 = 9.2 × 10⁻⁴ T. Accept 9, 9.24, 9.240. (b)(i) 2 marks: q ÷ m = 2V ÷ B²r²; q ÷ m = 2 × 5.0 × 10³ ÷ ((9.2 × 10⁻⁴)² × 0.28²) (1); q ÷ m = 1.5 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ (1). Accept 2, 1.51, 1.507. Or consistent with (a).

errors: Velocity selector: v depends on E and B only.
